CONGRANT.TITLE: Collaborative Effort to Enhance Water Supply for Agriculture and Food Development through Educational Training of Hispanic Professionals
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Currently, there is limited representation of Hispanic in FANH sciences due to limited resources available to recruit and retain them in programs leading to careers in this area. The main purpose of this effort will be to attract and recruit Hispanic students into FANH and related sciences through exemplary outreach activities, K-12 summer experiences, summer internships, and social events. In order to retain the Hispanic students in the FANH sciences disciplines, we will utilize interactive class and lab modules, research-based hands-on experiences, mentoring, student led organization events, professional training sessions, and financial support in the form of research assistantships. The research will focus on water management among various sectors which include food, agriculture, and natural resource development. The research will enable students to interact and learn from professionals in the various sectors of FANH sciences, while also gaining the required knowledge to develop innovative methods that enhance water resource management. These efforts will directly support 64 high school students in summer enrichment camps, 16 undergraduate students through research-based experiences, 6 students through summer internships at USDA agencies, and 2 graduate students with research assistantship. Overall, the program will impact over 8,000 K-12 students through outreach activities and summer camps with over 1,000 undergraduate students in Engineering and Science through designated courses, technical talks, and other professional and social events. We plan to increase the number of students pursuing careers and research positions in FANH sciences through career guidance workshops, internship experiences, and graduate program scholarships. The RGV area is known for its rich agriculture history (sugar cane, citrus orchards and cattle ranching) and economy, and serves as a wonderful setting for promoting FANH sciences among Hispanic.

CONGRANT.TITLE: South Texas Industrial Assessment Center
CONTENT_GOAL: GOAL 17: Partnerships to achieve the Goal
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The US Department of Energy South Texas Industrial Assessment Center (ST-IAC) at UTRGV will provide assessments to small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to assist them with reducing costs in an extremely competitive environment. The assessments will focus on energy efficiency, productivity improvements, water management, cybersecurity, and sustainability, all supporting priorities to improve the resiliency of operations using renewables, decarbonization, and energy storage.

Over 90 students have been supported from all College departments thus far. Four faculty and two staff are funded. Cumulative funding exceeds +$3.2M at the present time. Of note is that the center is sustainably funded for most likely the next 40 years at increasing multi-million dollar levels of support. Furthermore, an industrial assessment lab was developed and funded.

The IAC is directly and uniquely written into the Infrastructure Law (there is no other center or initiative at UTRGV written into the infrastructure law). Legislation H.R. 3684 enacted in the summer of 2022 funded with $550M directly supporting the IAC efforts in Energy Efficiency. This recently enacted Act provides opportunities to reinforce the academic efforts of our UTRGV College of Engineering and Computer Science, by supporting the activities of the IAC.

In addition, all manufacturers now have the opportunity to apply for $400M (a max of $300K to each company) in support for implementations as developed by the Industrial Assessment Center team.

Note the IAC program name has been changed ​to the Industrial Training and Assessment Center (ITAC) effective 2025.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Track 4 - Phase II: Center for Broadening Participation in Engineering: Engage, Educate, Enrich, Examine (CBPE-E4)
Development of fluid flow equation for flow through porous medium and fracture network using synthetic media
CONGRANT.SPONORG: American Chemical Society Petroleum Research Fund
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: While there has been extensive research on understanding fluid flow in porous media, the majority of these have used complex porous media samples from outcrops or actual reservoirs, resulting in failure to account accurately for the fundamental impact of various pore parameters on fluid flow. There have been studies on the impact of fractures on fluid flow but have faced similar issues due to lack of control on fracture patterns and structural parameters. Hence, our study aims to create a controlled porous structure with the inclusion of fractures in order to determine the underlying mechanism controlling fluid flow in such porous structure networks, which will capture the impact of various porous structure parameters on fluid flow. As a result of this study, a comprehensive model will be developed that will accurately predict fluid flow in porous media and fracture networks. This will enable more accurate oil and gas production rate estimation from various pore structure reservoirs in addition to reservoirs with natural or induced fractures. Furthermore, this research will promote further research on strategies to generate porous structures, including fractures that maximize productivity from reservoirs.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Understanding nanofluid reactive transport through porous media.
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Nanoparticles have found extensive applications in various disciplines involving flow of these particles in suspensions through porous media with even reaction involved in several application. However, due to complexity of pore structures, nanoparticle properties, and focus on applications, there is a need for fundamental research to understand and quantify impact of parameters on optimization of nanoparticle applications. This proposed cutting-edge research will study nanoparticle flow in controlled flow geometries using synthetic porous media samples to capture effect of pore structure on fluid flow without competing chemical properties. Additionally, we will account for the effect of chemical properties of porous media and nanoparticles on fluid flow along with impact of reactive flow on nanoparticle flow in controlled synthetic porous media to capture interaction of reaction and nanoparticle transport. Through both experimental and modeling work, this study will be able to produce a more accurate predictive model of reactive nanofluid flow in porous media.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Assessment and Planning of Decarbonization Research and Training at UTRGV
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: We will conduct an R&D scoping study and university self-assessment to evaluate how the university’s current capabilities, expertise, personnel, facilities and equipment, aligned with FECM objectives. Afterwards, we will identify gaps in capabilities and provide a plan to better prepare UTRGV for potential future competitive solicitations focused on FECM supported technologies.  The first objective of this project is to assess existing UTRGV research thrust areas and associated resource capabilities relevant to the mission of FECM to meet the decarbonization goals set for 2035 and 2050. Data on the level of expertise of the relevant faculty/researchers in the focus research areas along with current awards received from all federal agencies on decarbonization research since January 2017 will be collected. Then available faculty expertise, laboratory equipment and other resource capabilities, relevant course offerings and curriculum will be assessed. Afterwards, the focus will be on second objective, which is to assess missing resources to become more competitive in obtaining R&D grants. This objective will involve providing an estimate of the number, relevant experience, and cost of personnel necessary along with how the existing equipment could be modified – and the associated cost – to build the required interdisciplinary team to improve UTRGV’s competitiveness to address future FECM research related opportunities. The overarching objective is to develop student training & education plan to ensure UTRGV’s minority students are prepared to conduct R&D projects. Within this objective, current academic courses, programs, and/or curriculum that aligns with FECM goals will be assessed and then will identify, describe, and develop additional student training. Aligned with this, partner institution, LSU will provide support on student training, including a specialized course on decarbonization, to fill the gaps in our curriculum in a timely manner. The team will also suggest ways in which FECM may support the professional development of minority students from underrepresented and structurally marginalized communities of Rio Grande Valley.

CONGRANT.TITLE: MRI: Acquisition of a Scanning Transmission Electron Microscope (STEM) for Advanced Materials Research and Education Programs at the Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
PROJECT SUMMARY

Overview:
The objective of the present MRI proposal is to acquire a state-of-the-art Scanning Transmission Electron Microscope (STEM) that will support interdisciplinary research and education programs at UTRGV. The STEM combines the principles of transmission electron microscopy and scanning electron microscopy. The proposed instrument (Talos™ F200i) is flexible and compact 200 kV Field Emission Gun (FEG) STEM, designed for precise and quantitative characterization of nanomaterials and biological cells. It combines an outstanding quality in high-resolution STEM imaging with Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS). In addition, the instrument is equipped with tomographic capabilities via software for alignment of a tomographic series of images, and 3D reconstruction of the data.

Intellectual Merit:
The acquisition of the Talos™ F200i STEM instrument will enable a significant enhancement of basic research toolset across a wide range of materials, medical education and research programs including Chemistry, Physics, Medicine and Mechanical, Electrical and Manufacturing Engineering at UTRGV. Specifically, the proposed equipment will support projects to advance the development and characterization of different nanoparticles as lubricant additives, composite nanofibers, high entropy alloys (HEA) prepared by Selective Laser Melting technology, regenerative medicine, polymers, and nanomaterials for use in , patterned magnetic arrays, temperature controlled drug delivery systems, bioimaging, nanostructured energetic devices, semiconductors, high temperature superconductors, and radiation induced functional materials. The acquisition of the STEM will broaden the research scope for all participants, making it possible to address new scientific challenges in new transformative research directions.

Broader Impacts:
This proposal brings together a diverse group of faculty members and will significantly impact UTRGV transition towards an emerging research institution. In addition, most of the projects will be carried out by undergraduate and M.S. students. Specifically, the instrument will strengthen existing courses and several more will be developed as a result of this funding. Additionally, it will significantly support research and education programs operated at the DoD I-DREAM4D Consortium, which was recently funded by DoD on a $4 million grant and NSF PREM funded projects. It can also be integrated in the K12 outreach and education efforts organized by the colleges and the consortium at national scale. Results from the research projects supported by this instrument will be disseminated in peer journal articles and national/international conferences to stimulate further understanding and progress of the various research areas of the investigators discussed in this proposal. More importantly, this proposal will:1) Promote a hands-on, entrepreneurial, educational experience, and training of graduate and undergraduate students in advanced materials, nanomaterial design, biomaterials and characterization; 2) Enhance the research infrastructure at UTRGV; 3) Enhance the interdisciplinary research partnership between different departments at UTRGV to better compete for external funding; and 4) Increase the Hispanic Student retention rate at UTRGV

In summary, the Talos™ F200i instrument acquisition will strengthen the existing materials and medical research infrastructure at UTRGV and enhance the research and educational experiences of many students at UTRGV and South Texas region.

CONGRANT.TITLE: 2021 Texas Prefreshman Engineering Program (TexPREP) Engineering Ambassadors
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The Engineering Ambassadors program sponsored by the Halliburton Foundation was designed years ago to recruit top engineering students as summer mentors for Texas Prefreshman Engineering Program (TexPREP). Dr. Stephen Crown (PI) is Professor of Mechanical Engineering and TexPREP Director at UTRGV, which provides 600 top middle/high school students a challenging seven-week academic program that prepares them for careers in STEM. TexPREP goals are to increase the number of students from underrepresented groups (over 40% female, 95% Hispanic and 65% low-income) entering STEM fields; reinforce students’ math preparation; increase college retention; and acquaint students with STEM careers. Ambassadors (engineering and STEM undergrads, expressing interest in oil & gas and 3.0+ GPA) gain valuable leadership experience assisting TexPREP participants with courses and engineering projects throughout the summer program and act as excellent role models for them. Ambassadors participate in a 2-day engineering lab experience with the U.T. Center for Railway Safety directed by Dr. Tarawneh, attend a virtual meeting (via Zoom or Microsoft Teams) with a Halliburton representative to explore employment opportunities, and are encouraged to take a course offered by Dr. Pournik (Petrophysics, drilling and completion, reservoir and production, and natural gas engineering). These opportunities will shape their career paths and give the Ambassadors a rich experience to share with TexPREP students.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Community, Innovation, and Resilience Program
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The “Community, Innovation, & Resilience” program will foster intercultural dialogue among the participants as they identify issues or problems in the Rio Grande Valley region of South Texas and work together to provide potential solutions using science and engineering concepts, which is a priority topic. The participants from Iran, Iraq, and Oman will learn about this region and work with the UTRGV participants to tackle real problems. In this process, the usual narrative is flipped, as students from the Middle East will provide assistance to local technical problems in the USA. This program will use free, mobile communication software such as WhatsApp. Facilitators will guide participant teams through a series of dialogues designed to identify a problem, research possible solutions, and present a proposal. The purpose of this program is to provide participants with an educational experience that both fosters intercultural understanding and real-world design engineering. The program will embed the Virtual Exchange university courses in STEM disciplines. The deliverables for the Virtual Exchange projects will be limited in scope and will be paced over several weeks to allow students to communicate and interact with one another at each stage. UTRGV launched a VE program in the summer of 2020 with an initial cohort of three professors paired with three professors from foreign partner institutions. Three more pairs are receiving training now for Spring 2021. This program was funded by the Undergraduate International Studies and Foreign Languages Program of the US Dept of Ed, which is ending in November 2020. We hope to expand and continue this program through the Stevens Initiative grant. A priority for this project is to train and establish virtual exchange facilitators that offer recurring university courses. Faculty learning groups will allow facilitators to support each other after the grant ends.

Incorporating Hands-On Energy Related Experiments in the College of Engineering to Enhance Understanding
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Several fundamental petroleum engineering related experimental setups will be developed by a group of engineering students in the Fall of 2021 and Spring 2022. Through strong outreach program, around 16 under-represented minority undergraduate students (over 90% Hispanic) with at least 25% of them being female will be engaged in these setups. The developed experiments will be incorporated into the four courses in the Petroleum Engineering Certificate Program with utilization of the experiments in Spring 2022 and Fall 2022 (enrollment in each course is on average about 20 students). In addition, there will be several open days for the lab, where experienced students will demonstrate those experiments to the general engineering student body (over 800 students) in addition the allowing Society of Petroleum Engineers (SPE) student chapter to utilize the facility to promote interest in the field to engineering students. Furthermore, in order to promote engineering, especially interest in the oil and gas sector, during the spring semester, when middle and high school students (around 200) from various school districts visit the campus, the lab will be open and experiments will be demonstrated to them. In the summer, when several K-12 camps occur on campus (around 200), especially in the engineering college, we will hold sessions to showcase the experiments to the campers to promote greater interest in pursuing study in disciplines that relate to the oil and gas industry.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Waterless fracturing utilizing CO2 stabilized with nanoparticles
Planning Grant: Engineering Research Center for Water Conservation/Management among Energy Industry, Agriculture, and Municipality
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The proposed ERC vision will be to develop a complete infrastructure for water conservation and management among energy industry, agriculture, and municipalities. There will be detailed water analysis on produced water and fracture fluid return from energy industry, water runoff from agriculture use, and greywater from municipality. The analysis will be summarized into a matrix that groups similar quality water products in order to generate a better perspective and overview of various water supplies. The next phase will be to employ various treatment strategies and determine the resulting water quality. These data will also be summarized in order to get a better perspective on achievements of each treatment technique. Based on literature review and detailed study on quality of water required for various applications (energy industry including petroleum (oil and gas), geothermal, agriculture, and municipality), a selection matrix will be developed on how the treated water can be utilized. A detailed study on the proximity of various industries will be conducted throughout the nation with emphasis on areas with greater density of oil and gas industry and agriculture. This analysis will indicate most optimal locations for synergy among the various stakeholders with greatest economical and societal impact. The impact of this water conservation/management on reduction of water disposal sites with possible contamination and seismic activities will be studied. In addition, the project will determine if there is a need to develop new technology or to combine existing treatment strategies in a new manner in order to achieve the required water quality given the influent water quality. Based on that determination, there might be work on developing those new methods to achieve the required objective. Furthermore, the quantity of water that can be conserved/managed among the various sectors nationwide will be determined, as that will measure the impact of this collaborative effort.

Matrix Acidizing in Carbonate Formations

INTELLCONT_AUTH.INSTITUTION: University of Texas Rio Grande Valley

INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Matrix acidizing in carbonate reservoirs is a process that has been long used to increase productivity in oil and gas producing formations. The main goal is to create wormholes that bypass the damage in the formation. Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is the main acid used for this; however, it has several disadvantages that affect the success of these treatments. Its high reaction rate, inability to divert, and corrosive nature are a few of the reasons why research in this area has focused on finding alternative fluids. This paper discusses studies on successful alternatives to HCl. It has been observed that emulsified acids, which work with the addition of a surfactant to HCl, have shown positive results as their high viscosity allows them to retard the reaction rate between the acid and the rock and form effective and dominant wormholes. This is needed, especially in high-temperature environments. As HCl also lacks the ability to divert to low-permeability zones in highly heterogeneous formations, emulsified acids are also helpful for this task. While viscoelastic surfactants have been found to be less susceptible to form damage since they do not have any polymer content, their diversion performance has not been as effective as emulsified acids. Corrosion is one of the greatest and most expensive issues faced in matrix acidizing treatments. The use of corrosion inhibitors has been proposed as the best way to deal with this problem. Inorganic corrosion inhibitors are no longer an option as they are extremely toxic and pose a great danger to the environment. Organic corrosion inhibitors have been proposed as an alternative since the 1970s. However, organic compounds still pose a hazard in their use. Natural extracts as alternatives have been proposed for their inhibition ability. The use of henna extract and aqueous garlic peel extract as corrosion inhibitors has shown positive results with lower corrosion rates compared to some conventional inhibitors.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: New correlations to predict fracture conductivity based on the formation lithology
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Energy Sources, Part A: Recovery, Utilization, and Environmental Effects
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Acid fracturing is one of the most important well stimulation methods. Acid fracture conductivity, which represents the available capacity of the fluid pass in fractures, is one the main parameters for designing acid fracturing process. The volume of dissolved rock, rock strength, and closure stress on the fracture are the effective parameters on the acid fracturing conductivity. In this study, regarding above parameters and formation lithology, Genetic Algorithm was used to develop a robust intelligent model to estimate the fracture conductivity by considering experimental data of different formations. Results showed that formation lithology plays a considerable role in fracture conductivity prediction.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Simulation of dissolution front propagation during acid injection into porous media: a CFD approach
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Acid is often injected into porous media to dissolve rock material and enhance flow capability of the rock. Most simulation studies on the propagation of the dissolution front are based on constant injection rate (CIR). Therefore, the objective of this work is to develop numerical model to study acid dissolution front under constant injection pressure (CIP) and also incorporate the effect of fluid temperature on acid-rock interaction. Commercial computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) software (ANSYS Fluent) is used to solve three-dimensional acid-rock interaction model in cylindrical coordinates. In this work, correlated porosity and permeability distributions are generated. Effect of heat transfer between the injected fluid and the formation on fluid properties and surface reaction rate are accounted for in the model. The study confirmed that all types of acid dissolution patterns exist during constant injection pressure. CIP technique requires lower acid volume to achieve breakthrough in the conical and branched dissolution regimes, than that is required for CIR technique. In dominant wormhole pattern, both techniques require nearly the same acid volume to breakthrough. Thermal interaction between the injected fluid and the formation leads to change of surface reaction rate and physical properties of the fluid, such as viscosity, density, and diffusivity. Injection of cold fluid into heated formation leads to a higher wormhole density as found from experimental studies due to retardation of surface reaction rate. The model developed in this work accurately captures different dissolution patterns. The model shows that the acid volume required for wormhole breakthrough depends on the inlet conditions (CIR or CIP) and the thermal interaction between the injected fluid and formation. This modeling study attempts to answer the critical questions pertaining to the effect of temperature and injection conditions on acid-rock interaction.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Modeling Nanoparticles Effects on Optimization of Acid Dissolution Performance and Self-diverting in Carbonate Reservoirs and Compare it with Conventional Acid
Modeling of Aggregation and Gelation of Nanoparticles Using Quadrature Method of Moments
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Applications of Nanotechnology are growing significantly in the petroleum industry such as oil recovery, and well stimulation. In aqueous media, silica nanoparticles aggregate if there is sufficient attractive energy between nanoparticles. Aggregate size distribution evolves as aggregation continues, and once it spans the space, it forms a gel. The objective of this study is to study the aggregatio n and gelation kinetics in the batch. Population Balance equation (PBE) is used to model the kinetics of aggregation. Quadrature method of moments (QMOM) is used to convert the PBE with continuous distribution of nanoparticle size into a set of moment equa tions for efficient computation. The closure problem for moment transport equation is resolved using Gaussian Quadrature that requires estimation of roots orthogonal polynomials. Wheeler algorithm is then used for calculation of the coefficients of the rec ursive formula of the orthogonal polynomials. This study shows that the PBE and the QMOM along with the effective medium theory can be used to model the aggregation and gelation of nanoparticles at different conditions of salinity and concentration. The mo deled developed in this study is used to compare between the kinetics of aggregation and gelation of fumed silica and colloidal silica nanoparticles at the same conditions. The case studies presented show the unique behavior of fumed silica over colloidal silica nanoparticles for forming a gel network at significantly low concentration. This is basically due to the fractal structure of the fumed silica nanoparticles that has higher effective volume than the spherical particles of colloida l silica of the sam e size. The model also shows that there is a critical concentration of salt and nanoparticles above which the viscosity increase, and the gel network can be formed. The model developed in this study can be coupled with a transport model to simulate nanopar ticles transport aggregation and in situ gelation in porous media.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: New correlations to predict fracture conductivity based on the rock strength
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Journal of Petroleum Science and Engineering
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Acid fracturing is one of the applicable methods to stimulate oil and gas wells and increase the production rate in a carbonate reservoir. Acid fracture conductivity is an important parameter for the designing a fracture job. The amount of rock dissolved, fracture surface etching patterns, rock strength, and closure stress impact the resulting acid fracture conductivity. A model of acid fracture conductivity must accurately anticipate the fracture conductivity under closure stress. The rock strength affects substantially the fracture conductivity. A serious challenge of recent studies has been to predict the behaviour of different formations under various closure stresses. This study developed a robust intelligent model based on genetic algorithm to precisely predict the fracture conductivity by incorporating experimental data from various formations, whereby resulted in a good match between the model predictions and the experimental data. The effect of rock strength was investigated on the fracture conductivity under various closure stresses. The results show the rock strength plays a significant role when anticipating fracture conductivity, as various formations have behaved differently under different closure stresses. Furthermore, due to the complexity of rock behaviour at high closure stress, the results showed that as the closure stress increased the precision of all predictive correlations decreased considerably. Therefore, the fracture conductivity must be anticipated cautiously at high closure stresses by various predictive correlation particularly, in soft formation.

•	Identifies gaps in the coverage of the discipline in SPE programs and initiates efforts to fill them. 
•	Offers recommendations on P&O topics for SPE programs and volunteers to assist in program development.
